A beach on the Honduran island of Roatan, from where Angie Pena went missing on a jet ski in 2022 [File: AP Photo]By The Associated PressPublished On 10 Nov 202610 Nov 2026
A court in Honduras has delayed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Pena, a case that has raised concerns about impunity in transnational crimes.
On Monday, Honduras’s judiciary cited the need to review evidence and wait for the return of a court interpreter, who was out of the country. The decision has been delayed until November 20.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Honduran court drops case against ex-President Hernandez after Trump pardonlist 2 of 3Latest US military strike on alleged drug boat kills four in Caribbeanlist 3 of 3Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel?end of list
The verdict was expected that same day. Critics framed the unexpected delay as yet another hurdle in a case that has drawn comparisons to the crimes of the late Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender in the US accused of running a sex-trafficking ring.
Four men, including two US citizens, are on trial for crimes related to Pena’s disappearance four years ago.
Harold Green and William James Murdock, both from the US, face human-trafficking charges. Another US citizen, Gary Lee Johnston, and Honduran citizen Gustavo Trejo are accused of criminal association.
Honduran authorities have also sought an Interpol notice for another suspect, US citizen Antony Frank Grayson.
The Honduran public prosecutor’s office said the suspects are part of a network involved in crimes including drug trafficking and sex trafficking involving minors.

US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is probing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence services.
Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said law enforcement had began inquires following Huang’s admission that he engaged in an extramarital relationship with a Chinese executive named Alice Huang.

“He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him,” Trump said.

Lipan Apache tribe member Joey Montoya attends a rally in San Antonio, Texas, opposing border wall construction in Big Bend National Park on August 28, 2026 [File: Joel Angel Juarez/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
The United States Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to build a border wall through a remote section of Big Bend National Park in West Texas.
In its decision on Monday, the court granted the government’s emergency request to lift a lower court’s injunction that had paused construction while the matter was litigated.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump administration seeks Supreme Court approval to build Big Bend walllist 2 of 3Landowners in Texas ask court to stop Trump border walllist 3 of 3Tribe accuses US federal agents of ‘trespassing’ on indigenous border landend of list
The injunction, it said, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity”.
The border wall has long been a signature part of Trump’s platform to restrict immigration into the US.
During his first successful bid for the presidency in 2016, for instance, he rallied supporters with chants of “Build the wall!”
But the push to expand the border barrier through the popular national park has met pushback from conservationists, local officials and some members of Trump’s own Republican Party.
Big Bend National Park includes mountain ranges and desert that serve as a home to endangered species like the Mexican long-nosed bat.
Opponents say the plan to build the wall through the park would disrupt the ecologically and culturally significant landscape.

US President Donald Trump gestures after a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on November 9, 2026 [Mandel Ngan/AFP]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
United States President Donald Trump has signalled that he considers the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively” at an end, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister in Washington, DC.
In a surprise briefing on Monday, Trump reiterated his position that the US had destroyed Iran’s military. But his remarks suggested he faces pressure from allies in the Middle East to bring hostilities to a close.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Can new US task force stop flow of weapons to Iran?list 2 of 3France accuses Iran of cyberattack on supermarket fridgeslist 3 of 3Qatar PM meets with Trump for talks on ending war on Iranend of list
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” he said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
His comments followed a closed-door meeting with US Vice President JD Vance and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who hailed the progress in a post on social media.
“We discussed the situation in the region and ways to progress the US-Iran talks,” the prime minister said. “Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.”
Still, Trump acknowledged the “status quo” would involve continuing the US naval blockade against Iranian ports, as well as the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which seeks to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
